## Motivation {#motivation .unnumbered}

Let's start with an example. Suppose that you flip a fair coin three
times. The sample space for this experiment is

$$\Omega=\{H H H, H H T, H T H, H T T, T H H, T H T, T T H, T T T\} .$$

Since the coin is fair, we have that

$$P(\{H H H\})=P(\{H H T\})=\cdots=P(\{T T T\})=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}=\uline{\hspace{3em}}.%\frac{1}{8} .$$

Suppose that we are interested in a particular quantity associated to
the experiment, say the number of tails that we observe. This is of
course a random quantity. In particular, we can conveniently define a
function $X: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that counts the number of
tails. Precisely,

$$\begin{aligned}
& X(H H H)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& X(H H T)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& X(H T H)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& X(H T T)= \uline{\hspace{3em}}\\
& \vdots \\
& X(T T T)=\uline{\hspace{3em}}
\end{aligned}$$

Since the outcome of the experiment is random, the value that the
function $X$ takes is also random. That's why we call a function like
$X$ a random variable[^1]. $P$ induces through $X$ a probability
distribution on $\mathbb{R}$. In particular, we can easily see that the
probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is

$$\begin{aligned}
& P(X=0)=P(\{H H H\})=1 / 8 \\
& P(X=1)=P(\{H H T, H T H, T H H\})=3 / 8 \\
& P(X=2)=P(\{H T T, T H T, T T H\})=3 / 8 \\
& P(X=3)=P(\{T T T\})=1 / 8 \\
& P(X=\text { any other number })=0 .
\end{aligned}$$

## Introduction \[DS 3.1\] \[Lec 5\] {#sec:introduction}

We have defined probability (measure) for events. In the framework of
set theory, operations on sets are limited and we are in need of a more
flexible modeling strategy. In contrast to the set theory, the
mathematical theory of functions is mature and provides a convenient way
for characterizing uncertainty and randomness.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Random variable.**

A random variable (r.v.) is defined as a real function from sample space
$\Omega$ to real numbers $\bR$. Suppose the random variable $X$ is
associated with the sample space $\Omega$,
$$X(\omega): \Omega \to \bR.$$
:::

For any (measurable) event $A$,
$X(A) = \{X(\omega): \omega\in A\} \subset \bR$.

For any subset $B$ of $\bR$,
$X^{-1}(B) =\{\omega \in \Omega: X(\omega) \in B\}$ is an event.

::: center
![image](figures/rv){width=".65\\linewidth"}
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Define random variables to represent the outcomes of the experiment.

-   Toss a coin, $\Omega=\{H,T\}$, count the number of heads $X(H) =1$,
    $X(T)=0$.

-   Toss a coin multiple times, count the number of heads
    $\Omega=\{HHH,TTT\}$, $X(HHH) =3$, $X(THT)=1$.

-   Roll a die; take the number of 3's.

-   Human height measurement
:::

**Distribution.**

When a probability measure has been specified on the sample space of an
experiment, we can determine probabilities associated with the [possible
values of each random variable $X$]{.underline}.

Let $A$ be a subset of the real line such that $\{X \in A\}$ is an
event, and let $\mathbb{P}(X \in A)$ denote the probability that the
value of $X$ will belong to the subset $A$. Then $\mathbb{P}(X \in A)$
is equal to the probability that the outcome $s$ of the experiment will
be such that $X(s) \in A$. In symbols,
$$\mathbb{P}(X \in A) = \mathbb{P}(\{s: X(s) \in A\})$$

The *distribution* of $X$ is the collection of all probabilities of the
form $\mathbb{P}(X \in A)$ for all sets $A$ of real numbers such that
$\{X \in A \}$ is an event.

Now equipped with the notion of a distribution, we can consider events
in terms of values of the random variables, e.g. $E = \{X: X \ge 3\}$.

The theory of random variable is developed in two parts. The first part
is devoted to the discrete random variables, the second part is devoted
to the continuous random variables.

## Discrete random variables \[DS 3.1\] \[Lec 5\] {#sec:discr-rand-vari}

### Definition and Properties

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**discrete distribution.**

We say that a random variable $X$ has a *discrete distribution*, or that
$X$ is a *discrete random variable* if $X$ can take only a finite number
of different values.
:::

(We also sometimes say that $X$ is *distributed as* a discrete random
variable of a particular name. More on this later.) Using discrete
random variables, let's describe the entire process:

-   An experiment has random outcomes. (Sample space $\Omega$). Events
    are *collections* of outcomes.

    -   e.g. Flip coin 3 times. Getting all heads {HHH}, or getting
        exactly one tails {THH, HTH, HHT} are events.

-   Random variables encode the values associated with outcomes (maps it
    to the real line).

    -   e.g. RV $X$ that counts the number of heads in an experiment of
        three coin flips. $X$ is a discrete random variable.

-   Probability $\mathbb{P}(X \in A)$ measures the chances of a random
    variable $X$ being in set $A$. It is equivalent to
    $\mathbb{P}(\{w: X(w) \in A\}$)

    -   e.g. $A = \{ x: x \ge 1\}$ for RV $X$, and implicitly measures
        the *chances* of the event that 1 or more heads are obtained in
        the original coin flip experiment.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
For discrete random variable $X$, the probability function (pf) is
$$f(x) = \mathbb{P}(X=x)$$ for all $x\in \bR$. The pf is also called
probability mass function (pmf).
:::

How is a pmf related to events' probability? To compute the probability
of event $X \in E$, we simply add the probabilities of all the elements.
$$\mathbb{P}(X \in E) = \sum \nolimits_{x\in E} f(x).$$

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Support.** Support of $X$ is defined as (the *closure* of) the set
$\{x: f(x)>0\}$. Notation: $supp(X)$.
:::

Informally, the support is the values of $X$ for which there is nonzero
probability.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
It is useful to sketch a probability mass function (pmf). For the number
of heads in two coin flips:
:::

It is also useful to note:

-   if $x$ is not one of the possible values of $X$, then $f(x) = 0$.
    (Thus, we only need to consider the support of the random variable,
    instead of the entire set of real numbers $\bR$.)

-   $\sum\nolimits_{x\in \text{supp}(X)}f(x) = 1$.

-   $f(x) \in [0,1], \forall x \in \mathbb R$.

Lastly, looking ahead a bit, we'll be learning about *continuous* random
variables (say $X$) that can take values in an uncountably infinite set
(i.e., not discrete) of values. We can calculate the probability that a
continuous $X$ is in an interval $(a,b]$ (for $a<b$) as:
$$\mathbb{P}(X \in (a,b]) = \int_a^b f(x) dx,$$ for a *continuous*
probability function (called a probability density function, or pdf).

(Also notice that this implies that, for any single value
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, $P(X=x) = 0$! Weird, but we'll get used to this.)

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
What is $\mathbb{P}(X \in (a,b])$ if $X$ is a discrete random variable?
For example, if you flip two coins, and $X$ is the number of heads, what
is $\mathbb{P}(X
\in (0.5, 1])$? What about $\mathbb{P}(X \in (0,2])$?
:::

Note, it is possible for two random variables $X$ and $Y$ to have
nothing to do with each other, while having the same distribution (i.e.,
same probability mass function).

Suppose $X$ is the random variable denoting the number of heads in a
single dice roll. Also suppose $Y$ is the number of heads from a
subsequent roll. the distribution of $X$ will be the same as the
distribution of $Y$, but $Y$ is not like $X$ in any other way. (They are
clearly from completely different random experiments.)

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
What is the probability mass function of $X$ (and equivalently, of $Y$)?
:::

### Important Discrete Random Variables (pt 1) \[DS 3.1, DS 5\] \[Lec 5\] {#sec:important-cont-pt1}

**Discrete uniform distribution.**

Next, we will learn some 'named' discrete distributions that are
frequently used for probability modeling.

The symbol $\sim$ is an identifier for a random variable, and specifies
its pmf. In statistical jargon, we will say that a random variable has a
certain distribution to signify that it has a a certain pmf (or pdf).

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Bernoulli distribution.**

Suppose you have a coin that, when flipped once, has a probability
$p \in [0,1]$ of yielding a head. Let's call the event 'seeing heads' a
*success*. The random variable $X$ counts the number of heads: $$X =
   \begin{cases}
     1 & \text{ if heads } \\
     0 & \text{ if tails }.
   \end{cases}$$ We write $X\sim Bernoulli(p)$ or $X\sim Bern(p)$.
:::

The pmf of a Bernoulli random variable is $$f(x) =
 \begin{cases}
   p^x(1-p)^{1-x} & \text{ if } x \in\{0,1\}\\
   0 &\text{ if } x \not \in \{0,1\}.
 \end{cases}$$

We can also write the pmf succintly as $P(X=x) = f(x) =
 p^x(1-p)^{1-x}$. **Q:** Can you see why?

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Binomial distribution.**

Toss the same coin $n$ times; in each trial, call the outcome a RV
$X_i \sim
   Bern(p)$. Then, the number of heads $X$ we observe from $n$ coin
flips is $$X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i.$$ We write $X\sim Binom(n,\theta)$ or
$X\sim Bin(n,\theta)$.
:::

The pmf of a binomial random variable is $$f(x) =
 \begin{cases}
   {n \choose x} p^x(1-p)^{1-x} & \text{ if } x \in\{0,1,\cdots, n\}\\
   0 &\text{ if } x \not \in \{0,1,\cdots, n\} 
 \end{cases}$$ **Q:** Can you see why the binomial coefficient is used?

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Prove that $\sum_{x=0}^n f_X(x)=1$ for any binomial random variable.\
(Hint: use the binomial theorem.)
:::

### Expectation \[DS 4.1, DS 4.2\] \[Lec 5\] {#sec:important-cont-pt1}

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
An investor is considering buyingwhether or not to invest $\$18$ per
share in a stock for one year. The value of of this stock after one year
will be $18+X$, where $X$ is the amount by which the price changes over
the year. At present $X$ is unknown (or *random*) and the investor would
like to compute an "average value" for $X$ in order to compare the
return she expects from the investment to what she would get by putting
the $\$18$ in a bank at 5% interest.

What will be her average return at the bank? Is it random or
deterministic?
:::

The idea of finding an average value as in this example arises in many
applications that involve a random variable. One popular choice is what
we call the *mean* or *expected value* or *expectation*.

The intuition behind a *mean* of a random variable is that it is the
weighted average of the possible values of the random variable with the
weights equal to the probabilities.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Suppose that the change in price of the stock in the previous example is
a random variable $X$ that can assume only the four different values
$-2,0,1$, and $4$, and that $\mathbb{P}(X=-2)=0.1, \mathbb{P}(X=0)=0.4,
    \mathbb{P}(X=1)=0.3$, and $\mathbb{P}(X=4)=0.2$.

Then, what is the probability-weighted average of $X$? How does this
compare to the expected return at the bank?
:::

The calculation in this example generalizes easily to every random
variable that assumes only finitely many values.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Expectation.**

For discrete random variable $X$,
$$\mathbb{E}[X] =\sum \nolimits_{\text{All } x} x f(x) =  \sum \nolimits_{x \in supp(X)} x f(x),$$
provided $\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Find the expectation (mean) of the following random variables.

-   The random variable $X=c$ with probability 1.

-   Bernoulli random variable with parameter $p$.

-   Binomial random variable with parameter $n$ and $p$.
:::

Note: We will revisit expectation in greater detail in a later lecture.
In the meantime, you should read \[DS 4.1-4.2\] in advance.
